mainClaim: Cultivated meat could dramatically reduce environmental impact of food production while meeting protein demands
evidence: Tuomisto and Teixeira de Mattos (Environmental Science & Technology, 2011) ran a life cycle assessment of large-scale cultured meat production. They estimate that producing 1000 kg of cultured meat requires 26-33 GJ of energy, 367-521 cubic meters of water and 190-230 square meters of land, and emits 1900-2240 kg of CO2-equivalent. Compared with conventionally produced European meat, they find about 7-45% lower energy use (only poultry has lower energy use), 78-96% lower greenhouse gas emissions, 99% lower land use and 82-96% lower water use, depending on the product compared.
supportingPoints: Eliminates animal welfare concerns and zoonotic disease risks
Precision nutrition - can optimize fatty acid profiles and reduce harmful compounds
Reduces antibiotic use - livestock consume 70% of world's antibiotics
Food security - decouples protein production from land/water availability

sourceMetadata.title: Environmental Impacts of Cultured Meat Production
sourceMetadata.methodology: Life cycle assessment (modeled; assumes cyanobacteria hydrolysate as nutrient source)

limitations: The cited assessment is a 2011 model of a technology that did not yet exist at scale, and the authors note high uncertainty. It does not support price-parity or land-rewilding projections. Current production energy-intensive and expensive. Consumer acceptance uncertain. Disruption to livestock farmers and rural economies. Nutritional profile and long-term health effects need more study. Scale-up challenges remain.
